slides.title: Sputum culture
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Sputum (morning, after rinsing the mouth with water, into a sterile cup)

What it is used for: A sputum culture finds bacteria or fungi causing an infection of the lungs or airways, shows whether a chronic lung illness has worsened and whether treatment works, and helps diagnose pneumonia, tuberculosis and bronchiectasis. It is often done with a Gram stain. It is not usually used when a viral infection is suspected.

Physiology: Sputum (phlegm) is thick mucus made in the lungs; it is not saliva. It contains immune cells that fight foreign material. Its colour gives clues: clear — usually no infection; dark yellow or green — often a bacterial infection such as pneumonia; black — smoking or coal dust; brown — old blood; pink — pulmonary edema; red — needs urgent care.

slides.title: Sputum culture
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Interpreting the result
bullets: Positive result: An abnormal result may mean a bacterial or fungal infection; more tests may be needed to identify the exact type. The most common harmful bacteria found cause pneumonia, bronchitis and tuberculosis. It may also mean a flare-up of a chronic condition such as COPD or cystic fibrosis.

Positive result: A grown organism is tested for antibiotic sensitivity. Results: susceptible — the antibiotic stopped or killed it and may be a good choice; intermediate — it may work at a higher dose or more frequent dosing; resistant — it did not work and is not a good choice.
Negative result: A normal result means no harmful bacteria or fungi were found.

slides.title: Sputum culture
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: The test is often done in the morning. Rinse the mouth with water, then breathe deeply and cough deeply into a special cup; tapping on the chest can loosen sputum. If not enough comes up, a salty mist is used, then bronchoscopy. Drinking more water the night before and not eating for 1–2 hours before may be advised; before bronchoscopy, fasting for up to 12 hours.
Interferences: Antibiotics may affect bacterial growth and the culture result; tell the provider everything you take, but do not stop any medicine unless told to.
Limitations: Results usually take a few days but can take weeks for slow-growing bacteria. The provider interprets them together with symptoms, history and other tests.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Sputum (at least 3 specimens 8–24 hours apart, one early in the morning)

What it is used for: AFB tests are mainly used to diagnose active TB, especially after a positive TB screening test, an abnormal chest x-ray or symptoms; in people on treatment they show whether it is working and whether the person is still infectious. Symptoms of lung TB include a cough lasting three weeks or more, coughing up blood or sputum, chest pain, fever, night sweats and unexplained weight loss.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: Physiology: Acid-fast bacilli (AFB) are bacteria that cause tuberculosis and other mycobacterial infections such as leprosy. There are four tests: smear microscopy (results in 1–2 days but cannot diagnose); culture (confirms the diagnosis, but per MedlinePlus takes 6–8 weeks); a molecular test (NAAT — detects TB bacteria directly in sputum in under two hours and can check rifampicin resistance); and drug susceptibility testing.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: Per CDC, an optimal bacteriologic examination has five parts: specimen collection, transport and processing; AFB smear classification; direct detection of M. tuberculosis by nucleic acid amplification (with molecular detection of resistance where applicable); culture and identification; and drug susceptibility testing. Smears are stained and examined for AFB, with results due within 24 hours of collection. AFB seen are counted and graded 1+, 2+, 3+ or 4+ — the higher the grade, the more infectious the patient.

WHO recommends rapid diagnostic tests — molecular assays and biomarker-based point-of-care tests — as the initial test for everyone with signs and symptoms of TB; they give initial results within 48 hours of sample collection.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Interpreting the result
bullets: Positive result: A positive smear means TB or another mycobacterial infection is likely, but culture is needed to confirm: microscopy cannot tell M. tuberculosis from non-tuberculous mycobacteria. Because culture takes weeks, treatment may be started in the meantime. A positive NAAT means TB is probable.

Positive result: Culture is the gold standard for laboratory confirmation: growth of M. tuberculosis confirms TB disease. Drug susceptibility testing is done on the first positive culture; with risk factors for drug resistance or a positive smear or NAA result, specimens go immediately for molecular resistance testing.

Negative result: Negative smears do not exclude TB, and a negative culture does not necessarily rule it out — some patients are diagnosed on clinical grounds. A negative result can also mean there were not enough bacteria in the sample.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: At least three consecutive sputum specimens are examined, collected 8–24 hours apart with at least one early in the morning. Collect them in an airborne infection isolation room, a sputum booth or another isolated, well-ventilated area. Other methods include sputum induction, bronchoscopy and gastric washing.

Sputum is thick mucus coughed up from the lungs, not saliva. Breathe deeply, cough and spit into a sterile container. If not enough comes up, breathing a sterile saline mist can help; if that fails, bronchoscopy is done. Smear and culture are usually done at the same time.

Sputum is usually collected in the morning, and you may be asked to rinse your mouth with water first. The sample is thick sputum coughed up from the lungs, not saliva; the textbooks treat saliva or watery samples as unsuitable.

slides.title: Sputum AFB tests for TB: smear, culture, NAAT
slides.eyebrow: Body fluids and sputum · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Limitations: NAA and Xpert MTB/RIF results guide treatment and isolation decisions but do not replace AFB smear, culture, growth-based drug susceptibility testing and genotyping. All specimens should be cultured regardless of the smear result.

A positive TB blood test (IGRA) or skin test usually means TB infection but does not show active disease — chest x-ray and bacteriology are needed. Some people with TB disease test negative on these. When TB is the presumptive diagnosis, especially in a very ill patient, treatment is not delayed while waiting for bacteriology.

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
rows: none in 100 fields – negative; 1–9/100 – exact number; 10–99/100 – 1+; 1–10/field – 2+; >10/field – 3+ AFB count

slides.title: Per CDC, how is sputum collected when pulmonary TB is suspected?
options: One specimen at any time is enough
At least three specimens 8–24 hours apart, one early in the morning
A saliva sample in a shared ward
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: At least 3 consecutive specimens 8–24 hours apart, at least one early morning, in an isolated well-ventilated area.

slides.title: No AFB are seen on the sputum smear, but clinical suspicion is high. Correct conclusion?
options: TB is ruled out; no culture needed
Just repeat the smear in a month
TB is not excluded: culture the specimen and consider NAA
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. Culture is the gold standard and is done regardless of the smear.

Basis: Negative smears do not exclude TB; all specimens are cultured.

slides.title: The presence of which element is a typical sign of sputum:
In which lung diseases are fibrin, eosinophils, Curschmann spirals and Charcot-Leyden crystals found in the smear:
Clinical and diagnostic significance of sputum examination in respiratory diseases?
bullets: 1. Sputum analysis in lower respiratory tract diseases helps to determine the type of inflammation, the causative agent of infection and tumor cells.
2. Macroscopic: amount, character (mucoid, purulent, bloody), color, odor, layering, inclusions (Curschmann spirals, Dittrich plugs).

3. Microscopic: leukocytes and epithelium (specimen quality – many squamous epithelial cells indicate saliva contamination), eosinophils and Charcot-Leyden crystals (asthma, allergy, parasites), elastic fibers (destruction), fungi, atypical cells.
4. Bacterioscopy: Gram stain (bacterial pneumonia), Ziehl-Neelsen/auramine (tuberculosis); culture and susceptibility; molecular tests for tuberculosis.
5. Cytological examination – when lung cancer is suspected (sensitivity is limited, bronchoscopic material is preferred).

slides.title: Macroscopic and microscopic examination of sputum?
bullets: 1. Collection: in the morning, after rinsing the mouth, by deep cough into a sterile container; not saliva; for tuberculosis, several specimens.

2. Macroscopic: volume, consistency, character (mucoid, mucopurulent, purulent, bloody), color ("rusty" – lobar pneumonia), odor (putrid – abscess), layers, Curschmann spirals, Dittrich plugs, fibrinous casts.

3. Native microscopy: leukocytes, erythrocytes, epithelium (squamous – saliva contamination; columnar), alveolar macrophages (siderophages – heart failure), eosinophils, Charcot-Leyden crystals, elastic fibers, fungal elements.
4. Stained preparations: Gram, Ziehl-Neelsen/auramine, Romanowsky (cellular composition), cytological staining (tumor cells).
5. Interpretation: asthma – eosinophils, spirals, crystals; bacterial infection – neutrophils and bacteria; tuberculosis – AFB; tumor – atypical cells.

slides.title: Microscopic examination of sputum?
bullets: 1. Wet mount: from purulent, bloody flecks; leukocytes, erythrocytes, epithelium (many squamous epithelial cells – saliva contamination, low specimen quality), alveolar macrophages, elastic fibers (tissue destruction), Curschmann spirals, Charcot-Leyden crystals, fungal elements.
2. Gram staining: morphology of bacteria (gram-positive diplococci, etc.) and neutrophils – bacterial pneumonia; interpret together with culture.
3. Ziehl-Neelsen (or auramine) – acid-fast rods; result by grading ("scanty", 1+, 2+, 3+).
4. By Romanowsky – cellular composition (eosinophils – asthma/allergy), in cytological methods – atypical (tumor) cells.
5. Results are interpreted together with the clinical picture, culture and molecular tests; negative microscopy does not exclude tuberculosis.
